(Updates with market moves at the end of the day, and other changes, if any.)

The Nasdaq Composite sank into correction territory Thursday as mounting regulatory concerns for US data centers sparked a sell-off in technology stocks.

The Nasdaq shed 5.5% to close at 24,315, its biggest percentage drop in a single day since April 4 last year. The tech-heavy index entered the correction territory, having fallen 12% from its record peak reached on Oct. 6.

A 10% stock pullback from recent highs is considered the minimum threshold for a market correction.

The S&P 500 slumped 4.4% to 7,353.73, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average shed 3.4% to 51,523.06.

All sectors ended in the red, led by tech's 7.3% drop.

Shares of tech bellwether Nvidia (NVDA) tumbled 9.3%, the worst performer on the Dow. Semiconductor company Sandisk (SNDK) slid 22%, the steepest drop on the S&P 500. Other chipmakers also fell sharply, such as Advanced Micro Devices (AMD), Micron Technology (MU), and Marvell Technology (MRVL).

ING Bank sees potentially tighter data-center regulation following the Democratic Party's decisive victory in Tuesday's midterm elections.

"State-level policy will be more important to watch, as action is politically and practically easier at this level," ING said in a report Thursday. "The most likely approach is targeted regulation, much of which is already emerging. This includes data center-related taxes, reduced tax incentives, environmental standards, and requirements for developers to bear relevant cost increases."

Moratoriums on data center projects are unlikely to become mainstream, according to the brokerage.

"More broadly on AI, we expect the Democratic Party to increase scrutiny of technology companies, ... while utilizing the next two years to prepare an AI governance framework for 2028 and beyond," ING said.

Qualcomm (QCOM) plunged 9.5% as the chipmaker faces near-term margin headwinds from mounting data center investments amid component cost inflation, RBC Capital Markets said Thursday.

Applovin (APP) surged 31%, the best performer on the S&P 500, after the company posted stronger-than-expected third-quarter results.

West Texas Intermediate crude oil was up 3% at $90.73 a barrel in Thursday late-afternoon trade, while Brent climbed 4.1% to $98.50 a barrel, both rebounding after sharp declines in the previous session.

"A Democratic-controlled Congress could increase pressure to end the (US-Iran) conflict. However, no deal has been reached, and the two sides may still be far apart," Saxo Bank said in a report Thursday. "So far, oil has slumped more on hopes than concrete progress, leaving prices vulnerable to a rebound unless both Tehran and Washington signal a genuine willingness to compromise."

Treasury yields were lower, with the two-year rate down 12.3 basis points at 4.46% and the 10-year rate falling 5.7 basis points to 4.84%.

The Federal Reserve may need to continue raising interest rates to curb inflation, though at a gradual pace to minimize economic disruptions, Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack said Thursday.

"I expect that monetary policy will need to move to a restrictive stance to bring inflation back to 2% in a timely manner," Hammack said in remarks prepared for delivery at an event in Switzerland. "I prefer getting to that stance through more frequent smaller adjustments when possible, something which would be less disruptive to households, businesses, and financial markets."

Separately, Richmond Fed President Thomas Barkin said he expects further rate hikes, but is unsure of the scale and timing.

"Gradual makes sense if you think there's uncertainty in the world, and if you think that there's information you're going to get in the period," Barkin told CNBC. "And I think that's still a pace that makes sense to me."

Spot gold rose 1.1% to $4,103.38 per troy ounce, while silver edged up 0.3% to $52.45 per ounce.

COMMENTARY

The post-election rally lasted exactly one session. Chip stocks gave it all back on Thursday and then some.

Nvidia fell 8.7%, enough to wipe out its entire gain for the year. The stock now sits about 2% below where it started 2026, on pace for its worst annual showing since 2022. Broadcom dropped 9.3% and is also underwater for the year. The two biggest names in the AI chip trade have given investors nothing in ten months.

Micron and AMD each shed more than 15%. Sandisk, already down 7% on Wednesday, lost another 15%. The equipment names got hit just as hard: Lam Research fell 14%, Applied Materials 12%, KLA 11%.

The iShares Semiconductor ETF was down more than 12% at one point, its worst day since March 2020. The Nasdaq slid roughly 4% into its second correction of the year and the Dow lost 1,800 points.

So what cracked? Three things landed at once.

First, politics. Democrats swept both chambers in Tuesday's midterms, and investors are reading that as a tougher regulatory climate for data center construction. Voter opposition was already building, with freeze proposals floated in Texas. The market is now pricing in a slower, more expensive AI buildout.

Second, China. Beijing is dragging its feet on approving imports of Nvidia's H200 chips.

One stock. Nvidia-level potential. 30M+ investors trust Moby to find it first. Get the pick. Tap here.

Third, company-specific noise. Qualcomm issued a soft profit forecast and blamed rising component costs. Micron paused plans for a Taiwanese plant over labor disputes. Neither is an AI demand story, but in a selloff nobody waits to sort the details.

AMD CEO Lisa Su told Yahoo Finance the market is being "a little bit short-sighted" and that she sees no slowdown in AI chip demand.

So is the trade unwinding? The leaders are back to zero. The high fliers have halved. AMD is still up roughly 101% for the year and Micron about 148%, but both have surrendered around half their 2026 gains and sit more than 30% below their highs.

Zoom out and the picture is sharper. Nomura's Charlie McElligott tracks the big 2026 winning trades as themes, and all of them are getting unwound at once. The "semis-energy barbell," up 49% on the year, lost 9% over the past month and 8% in the past week alone. "Long AI enablers, short hyperscalers," up 34% YTD, is down 14% over the past month. And that's before Thursday.

title: Is Nvidia Still a Millionaire-Maker Stock?
detail:
Is Nvidia Still a Millionaire-Maker Stock?
Marc Guberti, The Motley Fool
Thu, November 5, 2026 at 1:11 PM PST 4 min read
NVDA
Trade NVIDIA on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Investing in Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) has already produced many millionaires. The leading AI chipmaker's shares have surged by more than 10,000% over the past decade. For investors who held on to their shares throughout that remarkable and sometimes volatile run, a position worth $10,000 at the start would have grown into one worth well over $1 million today.

However, investors shouldn't bet on Nvidia repeating that 100x performance, or anything close to it.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.
Its market cap is enormous

Nvidia now carries a $5 trillion market cap, and there's only so much capital to go around. A 10x return from here would result in a $50 trillion market cap. That's a larger figure than the U.S. national debt, and would be equivalent to about two-thirds of the current total value of the U.S. stock market.

This doesn't mean that Nvidia is an overvalued stock. In fact, far from it. Nvidia trades at a 13 forward P/E ratio, and revenue more than doubled year over year in its fiscal 2027 second quarter. The company also returned $26 billion to shareholders in that quarter through stock buybacks and dividends, but the majority of that capital went toward buybacks.

Nvidia is still the undisputed leader in AI processors. Its graphics processing units (GPUs) and other advanced chips are still integral for an industry that seems to be growing parabolically. However, its massive market cap will be a major obstacle to it producing another 10x return. It's easier to get millionaire-maker returns with small-cap and mid-cap stocks because there's simply more macroeconomic space for them to expand into. Even large-cap stocks with valuations below $100 billion offer much better shots at multibagger returns than a multitrillion-dollar mega-cap, as long as they are growing and improving their fundamentals.

Nvidia can still outpace the stock market

Finding a stock that could conceivably turn a $10,000 investment into a $1 million stake is extremely hard to do in any market, but if that's the type of potential you're looking for, Nvidia isn't the right pick. However, investors with larger portfolios who want to diversify their holdings on the path to a seven-figure net worth may want to consider the chipmaker.

On a forward price-to-earnings basis, its valuation is lower than average for the S&P 500, and Nvidia's growth rates outpace almost every stock in the index. That setup can help Nvidia's returns exceed what index fund investors receive.

Nintendo's Switch 2 sales are struggling. The Japanese games maker reported second-quarter results for the fiscal year ending March 2027 on Thursday, after the Tokyo close, and the numbers didn't help.

The July-to-September quarter missed LSEG consensus, per CNBC, on both revenue and net profit. Worse, operating and net profit both fell year on year, and the first-half numbers look strong mostly because Q1 carried a U.S. tariff refund.

Second-quarter operating margin was 16.5%, against 27.5% in Q1. IP was where they got some relief, rising to about $394 million in the first half from about $228 million a year earlier, a gain of roughly 73%.

Switch 2 shipments fell 41% year on year in Q2 to 2.67 million, after falling 34.4% in Q1 to 3.82 million. In other words, the unit seriously cannot catch a bid.

Regardless, Nintendo kept its 16.5 million unit target, which now needs 10.01 million in the second half. It might get there, with the holiday season coming and "The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time" remake out this week. That said, it's a big ask of consumers facing economic setback after economic setback. The first-half regional declines are downright terrible: Japan −39.6%, Americas −38.3%, Europe −39.6%, Other −30.1%.

It's not just Nintendo. PlayStation's PS5 is down 35% year on year, while Xbox hardware revenue is down some 15%. Sony shipped 2.6 million units in Q2, down from a revised 4 million a year earlier, per Sony's supplementary data released November 5. In the first half, shipments fell to 4.2 million from 6.5 million.

Everyone is getting hammered by price increases driven by AI, and specifically memory.

title: Why SK Hynix Plunged Today

Why SK Hynix Plunged Today
Billy Duberstein, The Motley Fool

SKHY
NVDA
Trade NVIDIA on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Shares of memory maker SK Hynix (NASDAQ:SKHY) plunged 13.4% on Thursday, amid a bloodbath for the broader semiconductor sector. It appears investors were caught off guard by the magnitude of the Democratic "wave" in Tuesday's midterm election, and now might be contemplating limits or bans on data center build-outs. Some post-election statements by Democratic lawmakers have also fed into those fears today.

Additionally, it appears that SK Hynix is having problems with the U.S. Commerce Department. The agency has continued to hold up export licenses for chipmaking equipment shipments to SK Hynix's NAND flash plants inside China.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Wedbush publishes a dour note on SK Hynix's China plant

In a note today, sell-side analyst Matt Bryson of Wedbush Securities wrote that the U.S. Commerce Department is holding up the export license for chipmaking equipment to be sent to SK Hynix's NAND flash facilities in China. Even though SK Hynix is a South Korean company, it appears the Commerce Department doesn't want leading-edge equipment being sent into the country. The controversy may also be holding up SK Hynix's plan to invest in a major manufacturing hub in New York.

If SK Hynix is restricted from importing the equipment, its supply could be curtailed relative to competitors in the NAND flash industry. Given the unprecedented memory and storage boom we are currently seeing, that could mean missed revenue and profit for the company.

Investors shouldn't feel too sorry for the company, however; after all, SK Hynix just reported absolutely booming results and is in the lead in HBM memory, the DRAM memory that's essential for the AI build-out.

Image source: The Motley Fool.

Breathtakingly cheap

After today's evisceration, SK Hynix now trades at under three times next year's earnings estimates. Clearly, investors don't believe those earnings will materialize, or that they will virtually disappear in 2028.

However, if data center and AI regulation winds up being less than feared, there is significant upside in SK Hynix, its memory cohorts, and semiconductors more broadly.
